utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-08-91-T. The Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, I'm Tom Hannis along with Gramsci De Fazio and Crispian Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, and Eugene O'Sullivan appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Aleksandar Aleksic appearing for Mr. Stojan Zupljanin's Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Would the usher please escort the witness back to the stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, good morning to you. We are at the stage where Mr. Zecevic would begin his re-examination and before he does that I would remind you you are still on your oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Bajagic. I have several questions for you today. Yesterday on page 20417 of the transcript, you were asked by Mr. Hannis a question about the public revenue service. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you are not an economist and that is quite clear. I'm only interested in one issue. As for the public accounting service in the former Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, did it exist in every town, that is to say every municipality in the territory of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from the highest level to the lowest, just as all other institutions. Any organ always existed at the municipal level, including the public accounting service.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bajagic, I will give you P189 in hard copy. It's a document which you commented on yesterday with the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I please have P189. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, before we begin to comment on this document, I would refer you to your paragraph 4 on page 93 which is entitled "MUP prisoners of war and prisoner of war camps." It's paragraph 291 of your expert report and further. Yesterday, you commented on paragraph 293 where you mentioned this document which we see before us now. However, I will ask you to comment briefly on paragraphs 295 and 304 of your report.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Relating to this document, instructions on the treatment of captured persons, in paragraph 295, I particularly referred to item 18 of these instructions, and I quoted by saying that corps commanders of the Army of the Serbian Republic of the Bosnia-Herzegovina were responsible for accommodating prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we just please see page 3 in B/C/S and second page in English on the screen so that we can follow what you are talking about right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead, Mr. Bajagic.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Considering item 18 of these instructions, I can repeat what I wrote in the particular paragraph in my report, namely that: "The corps commanders of the Army of Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina shall be responsible for camp organisation and quartering." I concluded in my paragraph 295 that it was the military organs who were responsible for the prisoner of war camps rather than the Ministry of the Interior. They were under the jurisdiction of the army rather than the Ministry of the Interior. In connection with that, I referred to the order of the commander of the Army of the Serbian Republic and some other documents which illustrate this by their contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you just very briefly comment your paragraph 304?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this paragraph I continued to provide illustrations and examples which show that it was Army of Republika Srpska which was in charge of these issues and I referred to a dispatch dated the 17th of June, 1992, which was entitled "Order to raise the combat readiness of the Birac Brigade to the command of the Eastern Bosnian corps." Inter alia, the order provides an estimate from the Main Staff that the Birac Brigade had almost 600 prisoners and that the corps command had not specified a location for the prisoner of war camp at the corps level.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, I understand that you are impatient to conclude your testimony but please be so kind as to have some understanding for interpreters and all of us. I cannot follow you in the Serbian language, let alone the interpreters who have to interpret you. Please be patient just a little while longer, we will not dwell on this too long. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the contents of this order and on the basis of an estimate, as it says, one can see that it was actually the corps command which was responsible for forming prisoner of war camps in the so-called centres for these prisons in the combat operation zone, that is to say in the territory which was covered and for -- which was covered by certain corps and for which the corps was responsible. I discussed it further on in this document on the basis of the documents which I mention at the beginning, including these instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: As for this order under Article 304 of your report, is it, in your view you, in accordance with item 18 of the previous document which we can see on the screen before us, that is to say the instructions issued by the Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it directly refers to item 18 of the instructions which we mentioned in the previous paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, yesterday on page 20382 when you were asked by Mr. Hannis and a suggestion that this document which we see before us now referred primarily to prisoners of war and prisoner of war camps, you answered in the affirmative and then you said in your answer: "However, if you look at the first page of this document, different terms have been used, not just prisoner of war camps, but also collection centres, and this is why this is also included in my report, and all these terms which appear in documents are also mentioned in my expert report." In connection with that, I would like us to comment on item 4 of this document P189. It is on the first page in both versions. Please go ahead but just please be slow, Mr. Bajagic.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I answered this question yesterday, I had in mind this very fact. As we can see, item 4 of these instructions uses the term "reception centres," and that was why I mentioned and emphasised that terms that we mentioned in the report are being used. They are to be found in various documents. These instructions are instructions on treatment of prisoners, and item 4 says that captured persons shall be taken to reception centres. Therefore, in the expert report I used various terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, on the basis of item 4, who determines where a reception centre would be situated?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we can see and as the instructions say in item 4, a commanding officer who is a company commander or somebody who is -- who holds an equal or higher position shall determine that before the start of combat activity, so that is the military rank responsible for this issue at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, a senior officer with a rank of company commander, does that refer to military personnel or not?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it refers to military personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, in item 2, can you please comment on item 2, or rather, paragraph 2 of item 4?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It discusses the further procedure that is paragraph 2 of item 4, further treatment of this category of persons. It says that their identity is to be established at the reception centre, and then in an organised manner and under escort they shall be taken to a prison camp. So procedure is further elaborated in the second paragraph, the manner of treating these persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: As for item 4, does it envisage two different institutions, let me put it that way, or not?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It implies the existence of a reception centre, that's the first possible situation when a person is captured, and it also implies that from reception centres, persons can be sent to prison camps, so it's not identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the following page in the Serbian version, paragraph 5, I'm interested in the first sentence of the first paragraph of item 5. I would like to hear your comment and then also the second paragraph of the same item. Can you please comment on that for us.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 5 mentions in the first sentence what is meant by a prison camp and also discusses the accommodation conditions which have to be the same as those provided to units billeted in the same area. It also says that conditions shall make allowance for the habits and customs of captured persons. If I understood this properly, I should also comment on the following sentence because that is paragraph 2. It talks about mixed camps in which separate dormitories and sanitation facilities shall be provided for female prisoners. So as I said, item 5 talks about creating certain living conditions in camps and some specific details which are important or specified, such as, for example, the issue of female prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, does item 5 mention prisoner of war camps or some other type of camp?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's clear from the first sentence, prison camps shall be taken to mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And if I understood properly, what is envisaged here is also what needs to be done when women should happen to be in this prison camps?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. It is the obligation to organise separate dormitories and sanitation facilities or, I suppose, conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I see that Mr. Hannis is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I had an objection to the form of the question because item 2 of this document makes clear who the captured persons are in the reception centre and these prison camps. Captured persons are members of enemy armed forces which can include females but we are talking about combatants.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I'm not sure I understand the objection. I think this is a submission and the submissions should be, I guess, at the very end of the case when we will give our prospective views on certain documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, I agree, but I would then ask you to clarify with the witness the discrepancy that seems to be included in this document, because it is clear from the wording of Article 1 -- sorry, Article 2 that this instruction is issued by the army and it is binding upon the armed members of the armed forces of the Republika Srpska and it is designed to treat or to deal with the treatment of captured combatants. And as Mr. Hannis pointed out, combatants may, of course, also include women. But then the question arises with the -- how female civilians to the extent in which they are captured, how they are treated and the larger issue behind this is how civilians who are captured are treated, and one issue or one question that I have is whether this instruction would also cover the treatment of civilian detainees and not only combatants.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, you heard the question of Judge Harhoff. I don't want to paraphrase it so well, could you please answer the question directly.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entire document, these instructions deal with the captured persons. Item 2 defines that term. Members of enemy armed forces will have surrendered and laid down their arms or have been overpowered and are out of combat, it is very clear, therefore, who this is about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But, Mr. Bajagic, the issue behind all of this is really if you can tell us about the legal framework that was in place at the time in Republika Srpska that covered the treatment of civilians who had been detained.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the chapter where I comment the matters concerning these camps, I cited documents that I had, and these are orders of the Main Staff of the VRS, of the corps, but I didn't make any separate comments about the laws or regulations that deal with this. These laws and regulations aren't present but the one piece of legislation that was the focus of my analysis is the Law on the -- on Internal Affairs, but it doesn't mention this matter. Of course, I analysed this law but also other laws and regulations that are important for the structure and functioning of the MUP, but in those laws and regulations I didn't find anything specific about this. I only studied documents that were able to shed some light on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Is your testimony then that as far as the detention of civilians during armed conflict there were no rules?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as these categories of persons are concerned, I mostly cited documents that were created in the system of the VRS, and I also cite other documents as mentioned in the footnotes. In other laws and regulations, I didn't find anything about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, the documents that you have described in chapter 4 in paragraph 291 and the following paragraphs in your report all seem to deal with the rules issued by the Main Staff of the VRS concerning the treatment of prisoners of war, and although you are not a lawyer by training, I believe that you have already shown that you have sufficient knowledge about these things to make a clear distinction between a prisoner of war and civilians. So my question to you again is: Since we have had evidence in this trial about the detention of a large number of civilians and since you are an expert on the MUP, the Court is interested in hearing your testimony about which rules then would apply to the detention of civilians, that is to say, of persons who are not combatants.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As we can see from this whole chapter, everything that has to do with these camps and the very analyses of the footnotes as well as the sources that I cited show that the MUP had no authority over these which means that they were under the direct responsibility of the VRS, all these that we have spoken about. Also in connection with paragraphs 295 and 304. I said that there is nothing special in the laws and regulations that provides for these types of treatment, but as I said yesterday, I analysed such a situation and some are in my report too, namely that the MUP often issued warnings that at local levels there are such situations, and the question was raised and forwarded to the highest levels of the authorities what should be done about it. There were also persons who were in some camps or collection centres or detained without the MUP immediately processing them, so there were such urgent issues at local level but I didn't find a document that shows that this was also in the jurisdiction of the MUP anywhere, in any document. It was the Crisis Staffs that decided about these matters or whatever the executive body of the authorities at local level was called at the time. I referred to dispatches and other documents of the ministry at several places in my report that show the ministry's desire to resolve this issue the way it should be resolved. It was the Crisis Staffs at local level that took care of these matters and were responsible for them. I hope this was clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. And forgive me for scratching further into this but you see, the protection of civilians is basically one of the most important functions of the MUP. So we would expect that someone who is an expert in the MUP or on the MUP would also pay some interests into how this function was carried out, even though, as you say, the MUP was not directly involved in the detention of civilians. So I realise that you may not be able to tell us out of your expertise just how the Crisis Staffs or the War Presidencies then treated civilians, or, rather, according to which rules or laws or regulations the Crisis Staffs or the War Presidencies handled the detention of civilians. But still, if you have any knowledge about this, even though it may fall outside the strict centre of your expertise, we would be grateful to hear it. And the options that seem logical to me is that either the rules that applied to the prisoners of war issued by the Main Staff of the VRS, either those rules were applied also to civilians by analogy, that's one option. The other option is that civilians were then treated -- detained civilians were then treated according to some other rules. And the third option is that there were no rules at all. Can you give us some indication as to what legal regime that applied to the detention of civilians regardless of who was responsible for it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not analyse this issue in this way in my report, but one thing is sure, in a number of documents that I cite in my expert report, I refer to the fact that the Ministry of the Interior insisted several times that this issue must be resolved, that a legal framework must be set up for treatment of these persons and bearing in mind what was happening in some territories, probably at the level of the local authorities. I found in the dispatches, and I have mentioned some documents of this type here, that the ministry launch an initiative for this issue to be resolved as efficiently as possible. I pointed out that the functioning of the ministry in an integrated manner was very difficult, and in some areas at the local level it was the Crisis Staffs who were dominant. Of course there were problems and there was also this legal vacuum, that is, the absence of laws and regulations providing for the treatment of all categories of persons, namely those categories that cannot be considered captured persons which is a phrase used in these military instructions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, your comment of paragraph 304, the second sentence that begins with the words, "An examination of the conduct of the dispatch." It was about taking care of such persons.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The dispatch we discussed and that is the preservation of combat readiness of the Birac Brigade --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down a little.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That they were responsible for the establishment of prisoner camps but also centres for displaced persons from combat zones, so everything that happens -- for everything that happens in a combat zone, it's the military organs that are responsible, that is the corps commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, how do you understand the term "displaced persons" from the zones of combat operations, are they persons who took part in combat operations for the opposing side?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the term displaced persons denotes civilians, not members of military formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Bajagic. No more questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Bajagic, thank you. Your examination is at an end. You are now released as a witness and we wish you a safe journey back to your home. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, is your next witness ready to come on immediately?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, but before that I would like to tender the expert report of Mr. Bajagic. Now, Your Honours, having heard the cross-examination of the -- of my learned friend of yesterday, the Defence is proposing that the Bajagic report be admitted partially, namely that all annexes, 1 to 11, because those are the annexes of the documents that he retyped himself, be taken out of his expert report. So, therefore, his expert report and Annex, 12 which he confirms he authored it himself, be admitted. I have the reference 1D numbers. It's 1D063016, that's expert report in Serbian -- in English, I'm sorry. And in Serbian, it's 1D062404. And his updated CV is 1D064993, is the English version, and the Serbian version is 1D064985. And, of course, we will provide the list with the footnotes which are not exhibits in this case at this point together to be admitted with the expert report. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours will recall that when we found our notice concerning the witness, we objected to certain specific portions of his report. We stand by those objections and, actually, based on his testimony now, it's the Prosecution's position that you should not accept any of his report, not only because of contents, but because of what you've learned about the level of his expertise, his methodology, the kinds of sources he relied on, et cetera. I would like the opportunity to file a written submission detailing this and also because the Defence is proposing to introduce all of the footnoted documents, I need an opportunity to address each of those because they weren't shown to the witness and they weren't discussed. But it's the Prosecution position that a number of those footnoted documents should not admissible for various reasons. There is some question about the source or authenticity of some of them. Many of them, we think, simply aren't relevant. They are in the portion of the report which we say is basically a tu quoque argument and therefore not relevant. So I would respectfully request that Your Honours defer a final decision on whether or not the report gets admitted at all or which portions you are going to admit until you've had an opportunity to review our written submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, with all due respect, the -- I think the purpose of the cross-examination of a party is to challenge precisely the documents based on which the conclusions were made, the conclusions and whatever the statement or actually whatever the position the expert took. So if it wasn't challenged during the cross-examination, Your Honours, it cannot be challenged through some other means by filing a motion to challenge it post facto when the witness left the court and finished his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I don't know whether I misunderstood Mr. Hannis, but I didn't appreciate what he said to be that he would be taking, as it were, a new challenge in his written motion. What I thought he was saying is that he was merely requesting time to organise it in a comprehensible written form and one of the -- I don't want to put words in Mr. Hannis' mouth, nor do I wish to anticipate what he may say in any written motion, but one of the principal planks, as I understand it, is that his challenge to the methodology which he did make in the cross-examination was so that it's so interwoven in the report and that is the basis on which he would take the extreme, for want of a better word, step of submitting that it should be rejected in its entirety. Did I understand you correctly, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm not sure, and let me make a few comments that hopefully will answer that question. I note looking at the Prosecution's notice regarding the expert, in paragraph 5 at the time we said: "The Prosecution also challenges Dr. Bajagic's entire report, in general, due to his questionable methodology and source documents." So we are already on record as challenging the entire report. And what I was saying here in terms of written submissions, I did want to address some of the specific footnoted documents that are listed as sources for various reasons that I cited, but I did not address each one in cross-examining the witness, partly because you may recall once or twice Judge Harhoff asked me to get to the point, and I don't think anybody wanted me to go through all 495 footnotes and ask him about every one of those documents and some footnotes listed six or seven documents. But I don't want the Defence to be able to sweep in all those documents because I didn't take the time to ask about each and every one because I'm already on record as having objected about the source documents. And if I'm permitted to make a written submission, I will be able to address specifically the ones that I have the most concerns about. And if there's an you issue, the Defence thinks it's unfair I'm doing that way, and I suppose they could make an application to recall Mr. Bajagic to address a specific document. But largely the documents speak for themselves, and I think you can make a judgement once you have seen what we pointed out and what the Defence responds to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm even more confused than I was before, I must admit. I understand that Mr. Hannis' principal objection goes for the list of the footnotes, and I think that is a separate issue. We can discuss about the footnotes and the list of the footnotes, but the expert report, I hear that he said that in their submission they were challenging the certain portions of that report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I am sorry, I'll speak one more time and hopefully this will be the last time. We are objecting to the entire report, as I said, partly because of his methodology and what I think showed on his cross-examination, that he does have some bias, that the level of his expertise with regard to his apparent knowledge about certain things in the MUP is not what you might have expected given his work experience, his employment in the MUP, and his degree, and the courses that he teaches. But some rather pedestrian terms and concepts related to the MUP that I think we all have some familiarity with now having sat in this case for as long as we have seemed somewhat strange to him and he seemed somewhat insecure in talking about some of those. So we object to the entire report and to all 12 annexes, including Annex 12. Those are my primary objections. But the footnoted documents include, for example, the book by Mr. Domagoj Margetic, we just don't think that's relevant. We also think given his -- Mr. Margetic's history, that he is too biased and prejudiced source to allow a book that he has written to come into evidence in this case, simply because Mr. Bajagic found that he was a source worthy of reliance upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, again Mr. Hannis is making a submission about the -- his understanding of the report and the findings of the expert, and I again emphasise that there is going to be the time for the submissions. Now we are talking about the document that we offered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Having heard what counsel have to say, the Chamber is of the view that the -- Mr. Hannis for the Prosecution should be -- may be permitted to make submissions on the admissibility of the footnotes only, not the entirety of the report. And, of course, such submissions as are made would invite and necessitate and allow a response from counsel for the Defence. So having regard to the fact that we must await the resolution of that, the basic application as to the admissibility of the report must abide the determination of that supplementary ancillary question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Just so I'm absolutely clear, Your Honour, then, from me, you only want my submissions as to particular footnoted documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I need to add nothing to what we filed in our notice in terms of the approximately 200 paragraphs of the report that which we took objection for various reasons related to them being in the nature of tu quoque, irrelevant, or beyond the scope of his expertise. I'll only --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: There's your motion and then there's, of course, the cross-examination which you have completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. May I inquire what the time-limit is for filing that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: How much time are you asking for?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could I have a week?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: That appears reasonable, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cvijetic, you were about to rise?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. Just to inform you that we informed the VWS that the witness should be ready at 9.00, so if you believe we should start before the break, I think that the witness is ready. And it is up to you to decide. It is quite all the same to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So could the usher please escort the witness in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Do you hear me in a language that you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Could you begin by giving the solemn declaration which the usher is going to hand to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. The Court thanks you for coming to the Tribunal to give your testimony. You have been called as a demographics expert by counsel for Mr. Stanisic, who you will see to your left, and you are giving testimony, as I said, as an expert. Could I, first of all, ask you to state your name and your date and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Stevo Pasalic, born on the 10th of January, 1951, in Vozuca, Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much. What is your current function?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm full university professor in eastern Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: In which discipline?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Demographics and social geography.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And where did you have -- where did you complete your education?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will start with primary education which I completed in my birth place, Vozuca, in 1966. After that, I completed teachers college in Travnik in 1970. After that, I completed the academy for pedagogy in Slavonski Brod in 1973. After that, having served the army, as was obligatory, I continued studies at the sciences and mathematics faculty in Novi Sad and I competed my studies in 1979. Immediately after that, I enrolled in masters level post-graduate studies at the sciences, natural sciences and mathematics faculty in Belgrade where I defended my masters thesis on the 13th of April, 1983. After that, my PhD thesis was approved at the natural sciences and mathematics faculty in Sarajevo. But due to the outbreak of the war, I had to file my PhD thesis again, this time at the natural sciences and mathematics faculty in Novi Sad. I defended my thesis on the 20th of March, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: In Novi Sad?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Pasalic, we have received an read your expert report which has been submitted in this trial, and I believe that the side calling you, that is to say the counsel for Mr. Stanisic, has asked for -- could you confirm, Mr. Zecevic, how much time you will need, or Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we requested ten hours for examining this expert witness. I will not promise firmly like the previous time with Ms. Ewa Tabeau that I will try to make it shorter, but I will try that anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cvijetic, we always appreciate the assistance of counsel. And the Prosecution, for cross-examination? MR. Di FAZIO: I've indicated six hours, but like Mr. Cvijetic, I'm hopeful that I might be able do it in a shorter period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We appreciate that as well of course. So, Mr. Pasalic, as you heard, the side calling you as asked for ten hours, the Prosecution has asked for six hours in cross-examination, and after completion of the Prosecution's cross-examination, the floor will be given back to Mr. Cvijetic for his redirect examination of you. During or after the examinations by the two sides in this trial, the Judges may, at all points, put questions to you directly in order to clarify aspects of your testimony. But tell us, Mr. Pasalic, have you ever testified before this Tribunal before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And have you given testimony about your expertise in other courts in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So this is the first time that you are giving testimony. In that case, Mr. Pasalic, allow me to just briefly explain to you how the proceedings in this court unfold. Each of our sessions last an hour and a half after which we need to take a break because the tapes for the recordings of the proceedings have to be changed. So every 90 minutes we will have a 20-minute break. We begin in the morning at 9.00 and we adjourn at a quarter to 2.00 in the afternoon. Since your testimony is going to last over several days, you will then be required to appear before this Chamber at 9.00 in this courtroom for the following days. Before I give the floor to Mr. Cvijetic, I would only remind you that having made the solemn declaration that you read out in the beginning, you have undertaken to speak the truth and nothing but the truth and only the truth and the whole truth, and I should remind you that there is a severe penalty for providing false or incomplete information to the Chamber. If you do so, you will expose yourself to the risk of being prosecuted for perjury. If you have any questions to us, please do not hesitate to put those questions to us right away and if you have no questions at this point, I think I'll just leave the floor to Mr. Cvijetic. Do you have a question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Cvijetic, the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Pasalic, good day once again.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Judge Harhoff, so to speak, began the introductory part which is obligatory in such situations because even though your CV was submitted alongside your report, it is useful for you to tell the Trial Chamber something about yourself live. You have already done so, in part, and as for the part which I believe to be relevant and which you have not been asked about, I will just ask you a few additional questions about that. Namely, what was left out is for you to enumerate just briefly where you have been employed up until now and up until the work that you are doing now, employed as a full professor in eastern Sarajevo. Can you just enumerate for us where you have worked up until now.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Defence attorney, Mr. Cvijetic. I began my career as a teacher in primary school in Zavidovici, in place where I lived from 1970 onwards. After that, I taught in secondary schools where I taught statistics and some other economic and geographical subjects. Then I was an expert advisor at the republic pedagogical institute seated in Zenica, and I worked that up until the outbreak of the war. From 1993 onwards, I was senior teaching assistant at the university in eastern Sarajevo, and from 1996, I was assistant professor at the faculty of theology in Banja Luka and at the same time at the university in eastern Sarajevo and at the teachers college in Bijeljina. Between 2001 and 2003, I performed the duty of deputy education minister in the government of Republika Srpska. And in 2004, I was appointed the first president of the republic council for demographic policy. I was appointed by the government of Republika Srpska. Simultaneously, I was appointed as a member of the commission for demographics and statistics of the academy of arts and sciences of Republika Srpska. And since 2008, I was a member of the executive board of the agency for higher education and ensuring the quality of education in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I'm performing this function to this day. As I told the Judges, I'm professionally engaged at the faculty in eastern Sarajevo as a full professor, and my field of expertise is demographics and social geography.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Just to recapitulate, at how many universities are you teaching at this moment?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: I'm fully employed at the university in eastern Sarajevo which has now been integrated in accordance with the Bologna process. But at the same time, I am engaged as a visiting professor at the university in Banja Luka and at the Singidunum University in Belgrade. It's the business faculty from Valjevo which is privately owned. They have all been integrated and organised in accordance with the Bologna Convention now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. You mentioned membership in the executive committee for the agency for the development of higher education and ensuring the quality of education in Bosnia-Herzegovina, does this agency cover all of Bosnia-Herzegovina? This is just my question.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a newly-established agency for the development of higher education ensuring the quality of education in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and it is part of a network of European agencies for higher education. It is the key agency for monitoring the development of higher education and accrediting high education institutions and licence -- issuing licensing for their study programmes so that they could work in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So this is the most important agency in the field of higher education and it is my pleasure that I'm one of the members of the executive committee of this agency.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Professor, does this agency have anything to do with Bologna? You know what I mean when I mention Bologna, I think that everyone knows what this refers to.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm just waiting for the proper time to start answering. Yes, of course, I think I said that it is part of the network of European agencies, and it's purview is based only on the Bologna process which Bosnia-Herzegovina signed as most other European countries, and now this Bologna convention it being implemented. We are making the first steps. But the agency has the key role in the development of higher education along the Bologna Convention principles.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Before the break I only have sufficient time for one additional question. Are you a member of any non-governmental organisations?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm the president and founder of the centre for population and social research which has been registered at the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it is seated in Zvornik where I am residing at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Can you just tell us in one sentence what does your centre do and what is its main purpose, but just be brief?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: If you would like me to say that in one sentence, then, globally speaking, it is the development of civil society in general from the population and demographics aspect, primarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: That is what I wanted to ask you, whether it is related with your main expertise field and profession.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I see what the time is, I would move to another topic anyway and it is the time to take the break, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Pasalic, although you would have only just started your testimony, the Court would have been sitting since 9.00 and it is time for the first of those breaks to which Judge Harhoff referred when he introduced you. So we would resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Pasalic, when I introduced you as a witness earlier today, I failed to mention one matter which is relevant to your testimony, and that is the fact that the Trial Chamber has assessed your curriculum vitae and has studied your report, and on this basis, the Chamber has decided to accept you as an expert witness in demography. The difference between testifying as an expert witness and an ordinary fact witness is that whereas fact witnesses can only testify objectively to the facts that they observed without making any comments about these facts, in contrast to that, expert witnesses are allowed and indeed required to make inferences from the material that they have studied in their expert reports and are also entitled and indeed required to draw conclusions from the facts that you have studied. So these are the conditions under which you will testify here. And maybe I should also add since I see that you are wearing -- that you are using a crutch, that if at any point you need to take a break, you can just ask for that and we will accommodate you. That's all for now. Back to you, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, maybe I omitted to say that Mr. Pasalic recently had a -- sustained injuries in a traffic accident and these are the consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pasalic, I'm going to ask you whether you have any international experience. Did you appear outside the borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Yes. I do have some international experience, of course to the extent the conditions allowed. But I do consider it very important that I took part in some international conferences, mostly about higher education and the Bologna process or some related topics with regard to Bosnia-Herzegovina. In October 2001, I attended an international conference in Strasbourg as a representative Bosnia-Herzegovina with Ms. Alamija Tanomic [phoen]. In 2002, I also attended an international conference about higher education in Lisbon, in April, where I was the only representative of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Let me add immediately that in the framework of these conferences, there was discussion comprising introductory presentations or discussions in which I also took part. Likewise, in 2002, I made an appearance at the Landek [phoen] University in Switzerland - that's a private school - and they had a private education for peace. And I headed the delegation for Bosnia-Herzegovina at that event with Ms. Meliha Alic, who was, until recently, the minister of education in the government of the Federation of BH. After that, I attended a number of international conferences and scientific gatherings mostly in the neighbouring countries such as Serbia or Croatia. So that to this day I have attending about a dozen scientific conferences and I also made presentations there that were published in scientific journals, some of which are on the EC lists and that is very important for university professors.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You probably noticed that I and the Trial Chamber, too, are interested in topics from the area of demography. Did you go to these neighbouring countries to discuss demographic matters?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, apart from the international conferences about higher education that covered the entire area of higher education and I always placed a special stress on the student population and structure of teaching staff and very few people deal with that. However, that's a matter very important for Bosnia-Herzegovina because the young population has undergone a certain transformation so that our contingents are smaller now. At scientific conferences in neighbouring countries, I took part in such events, both in Serbia and Croatia, and I discussed changes in rural areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I always took a -- singled out a municipality as a reference, in this case Foca; whereas in Serbia, I focused on the problems of the young population, the student population in Republika Srpska. And then there is a number of other works that I classified in accordance with the international APA standards which can be seen from my professional bibliography which is attached.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have any international appearances planned for this year?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Yes. There will be a lot of such activity. I consider my appearance here before this Tribunal very important, and I believe, or rather, I see it as a recognition for myself as a professor. But there are also some very serious international scientific congresses that will take place both in Bosnia-Herzegovina and beyond. I primarily refer to Croatia and Serbia, our neighbouring countries, where regularly attend such international conferences, but if I'm invited, I also go to other countries in the region or even beyond.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I believe that it was this year or late last year Ms. Ewa Tabeau had a book presentation in Belgrade. Were you invited?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was invited to the event. Unfortunately for health-related reasons, I couldn't attend but I was able to get a copy of Ms. Tabeau's book. I tried to reach the essence of her research in the short time that I have had this book and I think I'll be able to say more about that here. I have studied the works of Ewa Tabeau and some of her co-workers because there are very few works that deal with the processes in the war and in the post-war period in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So that I hope that in due time I will be able to use this information for my own research and publish a similar work as that of Ewa Tabeau, however, somewhat shorter because I don't have such logistic support in the form of institutions, et cetera, for such extensive research.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Professor, you have just mentioned something that I wanted to ask you about later, but I'll ask you now. Which authoritative sources from Bosnia-Herzegovina or other countries do acknowledge as authors that deserve attention when it comes to demographic changes and processes in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: I hope I will not be subjective in my answer. It is difficult to be very objective because we all have our personal opinions about these things. However, the most extensive research has so far been done by Ewa Tabeau and her co-workers and the information and documentation centre whose president is Mirsad Tokaca in Sarajevo. And without false modesty, I believe that my works must also be mentioned in this context. They -- their scope is a bit more modest but I couldn't access all sources necessary. However, all these works, including mine, can also be viewed critically.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we have already arrived at your work, so tell us briefly how many books you published, how many papers, and please single out only those that you consider relevant for the Trial Chamber and your work. I made a joke and when I suggested to you that you bring all these to The Hague and then you answered then you would need a truck in that case. So don't use a truck, just single out a few that deal with the area that we are interested in.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: I've so far published nine books, nine books of university significance. However, not all books are meant to be textbooks for students. Some are also meant for the general audience. I can single out two books that are important for the subject matter we are speaking about. I have one of them here, "The Suffering of Serbs and Serb Settlements in Bosnia-Herzegovina," which was published in 1997. I collected data from 1992 up until 1996 and I can state very briefly that after it's publication, in two months, or rather, within two months, eight and a half thousand persons read it online and it was rated as one of the ten top or most-read books on the Internet. The last thing I saw on the Internet is that it's now in 35th place, although it's been more than ten years since its publication. I have since amended a book of similar content which is titled, "The Anthropogenic Reality of the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina in the Period from 1992 through 2000." And that book was used for my expert report and I also have a copy here. This is as far as books go, but in our work, we -- or rather, as part of my work, we are obliged to take part in scientific conferences and I mention some two dozen papers, most of which deal with demographic matters. There's no need to read them out because you have had the opportunity to see that yourselves. I would just point out the demographic problems of the RS or the problems of natality which is a burning problem in not only Bosnia-Herzegovina but in all of Europe now. And at the conference of the academy of arts and sciences, I made a presentation about the natality and fertility of the young population, and so on. There are also the works that I mentioned that I presented in Serbia and Croatia. These works were very highly ranked. Professional or expert works are targeted at a young or general public, so I don't want to mention any in particular. The most relevant from the area of demography are scientific projects and research projects in which I have so far participated as the leader of some 20 or so projects with -- which were very highly ranked with, say, the Ministry of Science and Technology of Republika Srpska. And you can see in the enclosed bibliography that these projects were very significant. Let me mention that I'm the first head of a project team that deals with the development policy of the RS. That is the first work in Bosnia-Herzegovina albeit only one entity that endeavoured to deal with the current demographic problems that are extremely present in Bosnia-Herzegovina even in the post-war period because demographic loss has been great, both during the war and after it. We'll probably get the chance to discuss that. And then there are also some other very significant projects that you will be able to see on the list of my -- my bibliography list. You may have noticed that these works are mostly about the RS entity, but that is because they are public tenders where you apply under a coded name, they don't know who you are in reality, and then the process begins. Very few projects have been done in Bosnia-Herzegovina about this subject matter, so we couldn't apply for seats in these projects. Only recently did I apply through my NGO, I applied for a project about the fertility of the young population in Bosnia-Herzegovina, but we will see what the results of that project will be in the coming period. And then there are also scientific conferences mentioned here. I was the reviewer of some very significant papers that I mentioned in the bibliography and some works from the EC list or from journals that have the so-called SCI index.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In the proofing notes, you just noted that a subheading was omitted. We can conclude that you also were a tutor to candidates who were drafting their doctoral theses. That's in section D; am I right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Yes, you are. That's on page 79, after section D, published expert papers. The subheading is missing, stating that I was a tutor or co-tutor or member of a commission for the drafting of a masters or doctoral theses.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well, I'll finish this part with another question. Have you taken part in publish debates or polemics with colleagues, with co-experts? Did you -- did you take part in any confrontation of opinions in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: I'm one of those scientists and researchers or professors who accept such confrontation. Unfortunately, there are few of us in Bosnia-Herzegovina who deal with this subject matter, but almost daily I am present in the media in Bosnia-Herzegovina because they invite me to interpret some things that have to do with demographic processes in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I accept these invitations gladly and provide data if they are available to me. Those who have more intensively or in an expert fashion dealt with these matters in the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina are unfortunately no longer alive, but we still use their expert works. However, there are very few expert confrontations of opinions in the area of demography.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In the introductory part of your expert report, and let me state for the Trial Chamber that your work has been filed under 1D062149, and we'll start with the first page after the cover page. Let us first explain how you -- how you came to be commissioned as an expert in this trial. And my specific question to you is when the Stanisic Defence first set up contact with you as an expert for this subject matter?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: I think that initially they called me in around 2007, but it was a very short contact because at the time it was already known that I'm dealing with these issues and that I was perhaps the only one in Republika Srpska. So we had a brief contact about that and then we got in touch again last year when we talked about my possible view of these issues and the possibility of writing an expert report. I gladly accepted that but I offered my own concept the way I see these problems as I know them best, and I said that I would not deal with the issues that I do not really know much about and for which I do not think I'm competent, because I think that would be useful for anyone in these proceedings. So I offered a draft which the Defence accepted, and after that, I accepted to work on the report. We have it here after some methodological changes were applied to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: As for the draft which you offered us, did Defence add anything else as part of your task? Can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: I offered my draft to the Defence, but I think that there were some suggests which were given, namely that I should give an overview of the work of Ms. Ewa Tabeau and her associates, which I did in my report, and it's possible that there were some other technical details that were discussed. It was suggested that there should be division into paragraphs because otherwise it looked more like a scholarly publication in accordance with scholarly standards, but it was adjusted to the standards which are used at the Tribunal here, these were the minor suggestions from the Defence. But in the professional sense, in the sense of the field of expertise, the Defence didn't go into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did you receive works of Ms. Ewa Tabeau from the Defence, and if so, which documents did you receive?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: I did on two occasions. One of the works is here. They have certain numbers. I'm not sure how I should quote them here but these are works of Ms. Ewa Tabeau and her associates in the Slobodan Milosevic case and Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin case. I studied these works, I received a CD with an audio recording which I listened to. What I managed to get on my own, as I told you, is the book of Ms. Ewa Tabeau, "The War in Numbers: The War in the Former Yugoslavia." It has around 1200 pages and I just studied the parts of the book that deal with the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, at least up until now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: It has been suggested to me that I should ask you to speak a little bit more slowly so that the interpreters will be able to translate everything you say. Just tell me, have you -- MR. Di FAZIO: If Your Honours please, couldn't we have clarification of what was on the CD, please. I mean, it's there in the evidence, but you don't know what was on it. And for it to have meaning, you should know what was -- what the contents were.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was about to be my question, but Mr. Gramsci was faster.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Have you followed the appearances of Ms. Ewa Tabeau before we engaged you in this case as a professional and as a scholar? Did you follow her testimonies before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Yes. You know that the proceedings can be followed on the Internet, and I did it even before I was engaged by the Stanisic and Zupljanin Defence. I cannot remember the cases in which she testified that I was aware of, but I had some of that at my disposal and that includes the CD which includes her testimonies which I have listened to. Of course I followed her testimonies because these are problem areas that I find to be very interesting.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Just to be specific in answer to the Prosecutor's intervention, the CD has the recording of Ms. Tabeau's testimonies before this Tribunal and you have listened to that; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Fine. Professor, I will move on to something else. Please tell me whether demographics as a science has its branches or fields and what would be the branch that you are closest to. But, I apologise, before you answer my question so as to avoid any confusion, please tell the Trial Chamber and everyone else what you have on the desk before you. I think we still owe the explanation. What are the reports that you have in front of you?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: In addition to my own report which I have before me and the report relating to the Stanisic and Zupljanin case, which is before me, I also have my original book, "The Anthropological and Geographical Actuality in Bosnia-Herzegovina." I have the book from which I used statistical data directly while I wrote my report, that's "The Ethnic Composition of the Population of Bosnia-Herzegovina." I also have photocopies of some quotations from two books. "The Population of Bosnia-Herzegovina" is one and "The Population of Republika Srpska." I also used valid statistical data from these sources in my report. And, of course, I also have a full list of the census of population of Bosnia-Herzegovina according to the ethnic composition which was published in 1995 in Zagreb. If necessary, I will explain what it is; namely, the information concerning Bosnia-Herzegovina have not been published up until that time because of the outbreak of the war. It was only in 1998 that the federal statistics institute published statistical annual journal which includes the data from the publication which was published in 1995 in the Republic of Croatia in Zagreb. It is somewhat absurd for demographers or from our point of view, but due to the war and the circumstances, first we received the data published in another country rather than in Bosnia-Herzegovina itself. This is what I have before me today. Of course I brought some other sources with me, but the majority of the sources that I used was left behind because, as I have explained, it would have been impossible to transport them all to such a distance, especially as my movements are limited so that I would be able to transport such an amount of materials.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now I will go back to my question, if you don't remember, I will repeat. Does the demographics as a science have its branches or fields, and which of the fields is perhaps the one closest to your expertise?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: I will try not to talk as when I teach students. Of course demographics is the science on the population and has its own disciplines. But in the territory of the former Yugoslav Republics, we mostly study demographics as a general scientific discipline. There are no so-called narrow scientific fields, such as Ms. Ewa Tabeau is, I think, the statistical demographer, and so on. But within demographics everyone chooses, according to his own preferences, one of the discipline, whether this be the migrations of the population or the dynamics of population change or population policy or history or graphic demographics or a series of other disciplines. And then one focuses in one's papers on these fields, or perhaps it could be vital statistics including the birth-rate and the mortality rate of the population, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Professor, as for ethnic demographics, is knowledge of that discipline relevant for studying demographics in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: There is ethnic demographics and also ethnology, this is a difference that may be drawn. These are two very important disciplines within demographics as a science, and we have to emphasise both of these when we talk about Bosnia-Herzegovina because this is, from the historical point of view, a multi-ethnic area. The ethnic demographics is a study of people and its placement in one specific area and ethnology also studies people which focuses on customs, culture, and other characteristics of specific peoples. So by the definition, these are very important disciplines for Bosnia-Herzegovina and you can see from my report that an emphasis was placed on ethnodemographic movements and trends in Bosnia-Herzegovina before, during, and after the war. But I suppose we'll have occasion to discuss this in further detail later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. So what characterises the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina as you would define it, as briefly as you can?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Among the former Yugoslav Republics, Bosnia-Herzegovina has the most complex ethnodemographic characteristics. It is undoubtedly an issue that needs to be dealt with. In addition to the multi-ethnic characteristics of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the three constituent peoples and dozens of ethnic minorities which are precisely listed in the annual publications, this is what characterises Bosnia-Herzegovina. Where within the borders one can single out spaces where there are dominant ethnic groups but also areas where the ethnic groups have been mixed to a great degree. So very often it was figuratively said that in the ethnodemographic sense, the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina is like a leopard skin.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Professor, what are the main natural and social factors that influence the changes in the ethnic structure, distribution, and the general characteristics of the population in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: You can see in my report that I covered the entire 20th century when I discussed the ethnodemographic development in Bosnia-Herzegovina precisely because of the very complex natural and social factors which had an impact on the development of its population throughout the 20th century and also now in early 21st century. Namely, the natural factors are really varied. Bosnia-Herzegovina is a predominantly mountainous country, and in the mountain areas the living conditions were very harsh and the population was always subject to migrating, moving to big cities or moving out to neighbouring or third countries which I explained in great detail in my report. What is even more complex are the social conditions in Bosnia-Herzegovina. From the historical perspective, the peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina, if we take into account the history of the country, the historical facts, this is something that has to be taken into account whichever issue one deals with. There were always these migration trends and counter-trends. Generally, in the world migrations have their trends and counter-trends. What does that mean in this case? Serbs or Croats were always focused on the neighbouring countries, that is to say Serbia and Croatia throughout history. As for the Muslims, or now Bosniaks as they are called, they were focused towards Turkey so the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina is an emigration area exclusively up until this day. The population has always been moving out because of natural factors and numerous social factors which are historical focused on neighbouring countries, economic factors which are dominant to this day which we have proved through empirical research, some sociological factors, and certainly the ethnodemographic factors which we'll talk more about. I'm willing to elaborate even on the issues as the Trial Chamber has allowed, I believe, which are not covered by the report but which support my arguments about very intense migration movements in the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is to say, the emigration of the population in Bosnia-Herzegovina, their leaving of the area. To a much smaller degree, we have the moving in of people to Bosnia-Herzegovina which is immigration. So we say that the migration saldo is always negative in this area. MR. Di FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I'm not objecting but I just think that you ought to have a clarification or that Mr. Cvijetic ought to seek a clarification and that is on the use of the term "focused." The witness has said that: "Serbs and Croats were always focused on their neighbouring countries, that is to say Serbia and Croatia. And as for the Muslims or now Bosniaks ... they are always focused towards Turkey." Are we to understand that, that the word "focused" there means that they migrate or emigrate to those places? Serbs and Croats go to Serbia and Croatia, and Bosniaks and Muslims go to Turkey. It's important, I think, for us to understand that since the witness is using that terms, and the way I read that passage of evidence, I thought it was a reference to emigrate or migration to those places but it's not clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Professor, you have heard the intervention, I will not suggest to you how you should answer. Please explain this. And to ask you directly, which period did you have in mind when you said emigration to Turkey, which historical period did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Yes. Of course I will do that willingly. I had in mind a longer historical period. I don't directly have in mind the period of the latest war. This is why my report in the first chapter includes the historical or the ethnodemographic section on Bosnia-Herzegovina. These are valid statistical data which I included in my work, namely the percentages which were determined when censuses were carried out that the Serbs would move to Serbia, Croats to Croatia and Muslims in the direction of Turkey, as we said. But the percentages were much smaller than the percentage of Serbs and Croats were who were moving out to the two neighbouring countries, Serbia and Croatia. It is very precisely stated in my works but I thought that we would, during my testimony, reach the specific paragraphs which I am ready to explain and information contained therein. So we'll have an occasion to clarify every paragraph. Whatever I have included in my report I hope that can explain and clarify everything when answering the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: If I understood you well, the negative migration balance comes from the fact that much greater number leaves an area than is the number of people arriving to the area. Would you please help us, in one sentence?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Yes, you are quite right, but that pertains to Bosnia-Herzegovina in its entirety. Bosnia and Herzegovina as a whole has a negative migration balance on average, that's how it was up until the war. In 1992, between 13- to 17.000 people more left the area than came in, however this trend continues to this day and I can prove this with official statistical data. Let me be fully clear, I do not use any figures arbitrarily, I rely on the most reliable sources and the most relevant one is this statistical bureau of Bosnia-Herzegovina and other agencies of which there are three.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Professor, the frequent wars in Bosnia-Herzegovina did they affect migration of the population in that area?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Naturally. I would say that that is the key problem for the development of the population Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I will illustrate this with official data. Bosnia and Herzegovina is among the former, or rather, among the former Yugoslav Republic -- had the greatest war losses, which according to some data and all data is based on assessments we cannot have fully accurate data when it comes to war. In the First World War there were 320.000 lives lost and in the Second World War 700.000 lives were lost which was directly and indirectly caused by war. If necessary, I can clarify what is considered as war losses, demographic losses, and so on, which is very relevant for the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I think that this historical context in Bosnia and Herzegovina greatly affected the psychosis and the insecurity that existed in Bosnia and Herzegovina before the war and then when the most intense operations began, that also affected the movement of the population in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I hope we will get to that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly speak slower.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: We are now on paragraph 9 of your report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Pasalic, the interpreters kindly ask you to speak slowly because they have to interpret and if they don't catch what you say, the Chamber will never know. So please bear in mind that you have to speak slowly and distinctly and do not overlap with questions put to you by counsel from either side. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Professor, I'm now on paragraph 9 of your expert report. Would you please turn to that part. Under the table given by you, and this is where you speak about the factors that you just mentioned, you spoke about the political, economic, demographic factors and at the end you mention socio-political factors, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to know whether these same factors which were in place before the war also affected the war time migration of the population in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: As an illustration, I chose three municipalities, Zavidovici municipality, which is where I lived; that is to say that I directly participated in these events, and this is why I considered it relevant as I'm one of the best placed people to speak about these events. I also included Kljuc municipality and Sanski Most municipality which are all in the indictment in this case. What does statistical data speak of here? We had an official census in 1991 and then we had data for 2009 where we see the assessments coming from the Federal Bureau for Statistics concerning these three municipalities which exist within the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. All of these factors can best be illustrated by using these three municipalities as an example. As you can see, 1991 all three municipalities had greater population than in 2009. Naturally, Serbs moved out, as did Croats, and one could say, well, very well, the Bosniaks remained in that area and this is how this can be explained. However, it's not how it was. Five to 10.000 displaced people came to live in Zavidovici. They mostly came from Eastern Bosnia, predominantly from Srebrenica. In Kljuc municipality, also a number of displaced persons came to live, fewer than in Zavidovici. As for Sanski Most municipality, they had a large number of population in 1991, and that in 2009, they had 16.000 people left. Serbs and Croats moved out --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 16.000 people less in 2009.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Serbs and Croats moved out, and based on that, we can conclude that both during the war and after the war, the domicile Muslim population also moved out of this municipality. This confirms my thesis that economic factors were quite strong, both during the war and after the war, as were social, political and demographic factors. And, naturally, there was a factor called forced migration which is inevitable in any war, including Bosnia-Herzegovina. By illustrating these facts, this data, we will see that by way of this example I showed that it is not misplaced to criticise and to challenge data from the expert report of Madam Tabeau and also in the work of research and investigation centre of Mirsad Tokaca. Why do I mention these two persons? I do so because they conducted the most comprehensive research of these issues in Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is why I think my expert report complements their work and helps provide a more realistic picture of the situation in the demographic sense, both during the war and after the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And by your leave, I will paraphrase the words of Madam Tabeau. She and her associates when assessing or evaluating the project of the research and documentation centre of Mirsad Tokaca which is called "The Bosnian Book of the Dead." She said that it was very important to use a large number of sources, to use different methodology or methodological approaches. This is why it was quite sufficient for me to give a critical view of the work, both of this research and documentation centre and the work of Mrs. Tabeau. So this was a very polite comment by Mrs. Tabeau with which I fully agree because any war, including the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, causes a situation where final data is still not available when it comes to the victims of war and all of demographic processes. This requires very comprehensive research and this is something that Mrs. Tabeau also finally accepted and included in her work, and I share this opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: When I asked you whether these factors, the factors that I enumerated in the previous question which can be seen in paragraph 9, whether they affected the migration during the war, I wanted to focus on the following: Did this change the ranking of these conditions or these factors? Did some of them in this new situation become more dominant, more important than others? That's the point of my question.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: If I understood you well, you are referring to current contemporary factors. If we are speaking of current contemporary factors, then I would like to highlight the economic factors. All of our research in Bosnia-Herzegovina indicated that this is the main reason for all population movements and motivation for people moving out of Bosnia and Herzegovina, especially the young one in the age group between 20 and 40 years of age. And this is the most mobile segment of the population. And then political and some other factors are much less present when it comes to motives for leaving the area.
