We could add some other factors that also affect very intense migrational movements.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: As a follow-up question, Professor, let me ask you this: To what extent did the liberalisation of the visa regime for the European Union and some other non-European countries affect the movements of the population in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: This liberalisation of the visa regime was hailed by the population in Bosnia-Herzegovina, especially young and qualified workforce, who, for economic reasons, want to find better life outside of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Some of the research that we used, such as polls, questionnaires, and other recognised methods, including research conducted by me, among the most sensitive segment of the population which are the highly-educated residents, indicates that about 70 per cent of the young residents left Bosnia-Herzegovina mainly for economic reasons. Only a very small percentage, some 5 per cent of the residents, left the area out of political or some other reasons. Therefore, this liberalisation of the visa regime had quite an effect. On the other hands, we believe that it is unrealistic to expect people to leave at such a high rate because European countries are no longer immigration countries. They do not accept an unlimited number of immigrants. So a large number of people want to leave, but it is questionable whether they will, indeed, be able to leave. This opens up some other questions, how to keep this young and educated population in Bosnia and Herzegovina. However, this is not the focus of my testimony here today so I would not want to dwell on this any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let me put another question to you. Let us go back to the war events. In your expert report in paragraph 212 in some other places, you mentioned the so-called voluntary and forced migrations. Would you please explain that to the Trial Chamber. What do you have in mind when you say voluntary or spontaneous migration and when you say forced migration? Would you please define them.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Essentially, during the war, all migrations are mostly forced migrations. However, they can be divided into several categories and this is very important for this case. I wanted to highlight this in my work. It would have been better, perhaps, if I put voluntary under quotation marks. Using my own example, I voluntarily left the area where I lived in early 1992 when the war began. However, there was a dose of fear, a dose of insecurity, experience from previous war periods, especially in the areas where some ethnic groups were in minority. And then spontaneously, or under quotation marks, voluntarily, the population moved out even before the conflict arose. They moved either outside of Bosnia and Herzegovina or within Bosnia and Herzegovina to places where they felt safer. Every ethnic group mostly moved towards the area where their ethnic community was dominant. So the data from 1992 indicates that this transfer of the population was quite present in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I have to stress that this was not sufficiently explained both in the work of Mrs. Tabeau and in the work of Mr. Tokaca from the research and documentation centre. The movement, the transfer of the population in war time needs to be classified. This is not unknown in the world academic circles. There is ethnic cleansing. There is deportation and persecution of population. So we have ethnic cleansing, we have deportation, we have persecution and we have voluntary moving out under quotation marks. The ethnic cleansing indicates that the population was moved out by way of using force and quickly, and not all of the movement of the population can be classified under this category. This is why, in my opinion, it was very important to clarify this and to explain this further since this was not done either in the work of Mrs. Tabeau or in the work of other institutions. I keep mentioning the research and documentation centre, even though they don't seem to be the most relevant source for this case. During my testimony here if it is real relevant for you, I would like to spend more time explaining this phenomenon. So ethnic cleansing is only that phenomenon which encompasses that the population was moved out by way of using force and quickly. This is not something that happened in all areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina, especially not in all areas in the indictment in this case. There were also cases of transfer of population and deportation including regions where one or the other or the third ethnic community was dominant one. So this is how the people moved and I can assure you that this process continues to this very day.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Professor, when transfer of the population occurs, when a group of population leaves an area and comes to another area where people from their ethnic community have majority, does this cause the domino effect or does this cause the effect of connected vessels and does this effect movement of population from other ethnic communities?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: The way I see it and according to my research and this is confirmed by all statistical data, what happened during the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina is crucial. If, for example, and that's what I mention in some paragraphs, or rather, that's -- that was the way it was in the Bijeljina municipality, and I also explained why. Twenty-four thousand Muslims left the area, to put it mildly. At the same time, 39.000 Serbs settled in the Bijeljina area. That's what we call the connected vessels effect, or the domino effect, if you will. These are these spontaneous migrations that I mentioned. When one ethnic group arrives in an area, they simply take the settled areas of the ethnic group, that's in the minority there. This letter going to the areas that were left vacant after the departure of another ethnic group. These are the most intensive processes that happened in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I personally think -- although I don't want to go into the military aspect, I think that there was no institution that could have prevented these movements, mostly out of fear for themselves, for their families, for their survival, but also economically. Reserves of food were depleting and people were actually scared of starvation. And I can say that I've been through that. That was the situation in the town where I lived before the war. Such was the atmosphere before the -- before open conflict in many parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina because we must clearly point out that not every area was directly affected by the war. Indirectly yes, but not necessarily directly, and that's general knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Professor, you often use, and I'll state paragraphs 6 and 10 as a reference, the term ethnic territorial homogenisation. You use that term often, so could you please explain it to us?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Yes. All my explanations of the ethnodemographic movements in the war, and I also researched the post-war period, can corroborate the basic thesis that I put forward and that is the ethnic territorial homogenisation. This is not a known thing internationally. This happened from times of antiquity on, for economic reasons; in the middle ages, for religious reasons. During the colonisation of the Americas or Australia, Aboriginals and the native population was pushed back. In the 20th centuries, it was especially ethnic minorities that were suppressed, and thus we arrive at the period of 1992 through 1995 where this process was very pronounced. Ethnic territorial homogenisation means that the population of one, the other, and the third ethnic group was directed to those areas or regions in Bosnia-Herzegovina where one of these was dominant. That's for example, Central Bosnia for the Muslims, north-west Bosnia, or, more specifically, the Cazin region, and then the north-east Bosnia or the Tuzla region which is very densely populated, and, finally, Eastern Bosnia. The Serbs were oriented toward the Krajina where the concentration of that population was most prominent in the Banja Luka region. Then in north-east Bosnia, I'm referring to Semberija, Bijeljina, and so on, through Majevica, parts of Eastern Bosnia and Sarajevo Romanija area. The Croatian population was concentrated in Western Herzegovina, where nowadays there's a symbolic proportion of Serbs and Muslims, as well as in enclaves, in Central Bosnia, Zepce and the surrounding areas, and in Northern Bosnia parts of the Posavina, the areas of Odzak and Orasje. These are, today, those ethnic regions where one, the other, or the third ethnic group is dominant. I can corroborate that with a number of examples. I can give you the example of large cities such as Sarajevo, Banja Luka, Mostar, Zenica, Tuzla and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Professor, there's another term that you often use, you say that as a result of that there has been a simplification of the ethnic mosaic. Can you put that in relation to the leopard skin that you have mentioned. What would that map be like if we were to colour it using the colours that I usually use to represent the three ethnicities in Bosnia-Herzegovina? You know that there were those maps that were -- municipalities were represented in a certain colour standing for certain ethnicity. What would that map be like now if we were to colour it?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. At any rate it certainly would no longer be a genuine leopard skin. There were, or rather, there are individual colours that are dominant in certain areas, but there are still areas where the population is mixed. However, the process is in progress, it doesn't stop with the end of the war. In Bosnia-Herzegovina, it's still on-going, and this is something that is known from some international examples. Population is a dynamic category, and the shares of some group -- of individual groups change. In a couple of decades, the demographic image with regard to the distribution of population may change again, but we cannot know that. It is simplified now because the population is now ethnically concentrated. I must points out the following: Sarajevo is the capital city of Bosnia-Herzegovina and according to the information from the Federal Bureau of Statistics -- but I stress that these are estimates because there has been no census since 1991. We are the only ones in Europe who have been without one for 20 years, and that makes our scientific research more difficult because we lack valid statistical data. But according to estimates, Sarajevo is now populated by 90 per cent Bosniaks and the remaining 10 per cent are Serbs, Croats and others. Until the beginning of the war, the Muslims were dominant there but they did -- their share was not over 50 per cent. There were almost 40 per cent Serbs, and so on. This is sufficient example for the simplification of the ethnic mosaic in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Certainly, I can mention other examples too if you are interested, Banja Luka, Mostar or other towns can also serve as an example, but the situation is not the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Before the break, let me ask you this question: I will not speak about towns but in terms of regions. If you were to speak in terms of colours, where would a colour be most solid, ethnically speaking, in which region?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: I'll repeat, although I think I -- I've just explained. The Sarajevo Zenica region, so let's boil it down to Central Bosnia and this region is the back bone of Central Bosnia, has a dominant Muslim population. This is a very simplified image because Zenica was considered a very Yugoslav city until 1992, and Sarajevo, too, was multi-ethnic. The Tuzla region which is densely populated now has a symbolic share of other ethnic groups. On the other hand, the Banja Luka region has a dominant Serb share in the population. That was the case before, too, but it's more dominant now. Mostar, as you know, is still an ethnically divided town. On the one side there are Croats, on the other side there are Bosniaks. All of Western Herzegovina is basically a mono-ethnic area populated mostly by Croats, and a small share of Serbs or Bosniaks mostly no longer live there. This is merely an illustration of the regional ethnic situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina which speaks about very complex ethnodemographic movements, very complex. Many more researchers and institutions should deal with these matters so that we can come up with some opinions and offer some solutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, then that colour would be most solid in the area of the former Herceg-Bosna; am I right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Yes, Herceg-Bosna, but I've also mentioned some other examples: Sarajevo, Zenica, and these other regions, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I note the time, I believe it's time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we would resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, while we are waiting for the witness to come in, how much time do you expect you would be with this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, probably not have question for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Because he is joint expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, in relation to that matter, there is a question of scheduling of the next witness, Mr. Bjelosevic, who needs to return for -- and I was approached by VWS so as to indicate when would we expect Mr. Bjelosevic to return to The Hague. I am in -- I said that I'm in the hands of Trial Chamber on that matter because we still don't -- we are not sure when this witness will end. So I'm asking for some sort of a guidance from the Trial Chamber. I was -- I was -- my intention was to say Sunday because I believe he is supposed to start on Monday the 16th, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I was doing the calculations when this witness started, and it seems as if we are going to run into Monday with the present witness, so if Mr. Bjelosevic returns on Monday we should be able to pick him up on Tuesday. That is our estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honours. I will notify VWS accordingly. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Professor Pasalic, according to you, what is the starting point for serious demographic research, the basis?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: The inevitable starting point in demography is valid statistical data. That means that we need data that we obtain by relevant research, by the most relevant research. In Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is the population census. This is the so-called traditional approach of the population census. There's also a population census that is conducted by way of a population register which is applied by many countries in Europe and beyond. Other data make demographic research more difficult because they stem from institutions whose primary goal is not demography or valid demographic data. This has been the crucial problem we've been facing all this time in Bosnia-Herzegovina because, as I've already said, there has been no population census since 1991. And I'm talking about 20 years. It is well known that the information obtained by way of a population census is valid for five or seven years. Nine years later they are no longer valid or useable because they no longer reflect the realistic image of the situation on the ground, that applies to Bosnia-Herzegovina too. Apart from a database which is important for demographic research, there are also secondary sources which are also very important. Highly-ranked scientific papers, journals, projects, et cetera. If you have that at your disposal, then you can endeavour to make a comprehensive demographic research. But I must point out that in scientific research you cannot take everything from others. The most highly valued part of the job is what you research yourself and present in your work. This is usually done through empirical research, original scientific research in practice, and so on, which in my report is present and I believe that was the most valuable part of my research.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Professor, where do you think that polls or questionnaires and similar methods rank?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Yes. In scientific research, these are so-called tools, the tools that we use to research some events, especially where there are no primary data sources such as those obtained through a population census or other very reliable sources. Then you rely on these tools, especially polls, interviews, questionnaires. It is very important to choose your samples skillfully. There are many types of samples. They are determined mathematically, statistically for the sample to be representative and reflect the whole or the area that you -- that's the object of your research in order to depict the situation in that area as well as possible. But I must stress that it is very difficult to have a sample that would give a 100 per cent faithful presentation of the situation in a certain area or territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Professor, can final results within demographic research be obtained without a population census, and I'm specifically referring to Bosnia-Herzegovina now?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Well, I can start with a joke, maybe yes, maybe no. In Bosnia-Herzegovina, the census is the most relevant and the most comprehensive research conducted by statistical research and I have explained why. We have no more relevant source. With regard to the complexity of the subject matter, we cannot arrive at the most valid and most original works without a census, but of course, even without a census life doesn't stand still, then we use other methods. Currently, everything is based on estimates in my country, but estimates are like chewing gum, so somebody estimates that there have been 300.000 victims in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and then institutions are -- the most comprehensive research conducted by Ewa Tabeau and the IDC in Sarajevo mention a number of victims that amounts to one-third of that figure. So estimates are relative but we are still using them because without a census, there is no better data. That is why it's important to rely on a large number of sources in your research in order to avoid statistical subjectivity, bias, and in order to avoid creating wrong historic images of the situation in certain areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: It is not contested before this Tribunal, and you have also mentioned it, is the fact that the last census in former Yugoslavia and in Bosnia-Herzegovina was conducted in 1991. What I would like to know is whether there have been any censuses in the -- since in the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Let me point out immediately that according to international methodology, or, more specifically, the United Nations methodology because they determined the methodology that is binding on all countries in the world, and they -- the methodology also contains some guide-lines. But internal censuses are not prohibited in a territorial unit that is smaller than a country, but the Republika Srpska has not conducted a population census until 1996 when a rather comprehensive census of refugees and displaced persons was made. That data was very significant and it's still used for several purposes including research. There has -- the data of the number of refugees and displaced persons has been reviewed since and there are also different figures from the federal statistics bureau. And let me mention that at the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina there is also the statistical agency. These are the three organisations that are relevant for the publication of statistical data. And I mostly use the statistical data from these institutions if I can because other data -- using other data would be arbitrary and less than serious from the scientific point of view.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. According to the principles of statistical methods, by taking samples for certain municipalities, or just for one or several ethnic groups, could one draw from that and provide overall data for all of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: I believe this to be one of the crucial issues in these proceedings. As we explained all the demographic and all other complexities in the entire territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina creating any sample from specific municipalities which should represent the entirety of Bosnia-Herzegovina is practically impossible. This can be elaborated by giving a number of examples, including the ones from Ms. Tabeau's documents which I have studied where one can use good arguments to refute some of the conclusions which were drawn while admitting that great effort has been made and that this was huge work, this principle of work, statistical and mathematical, cannot be applied from a distance to such a complex ethnic and demographic space as Bosnia-Herzegovina is. That is why I emphasise that empirical research is something that is necessary when dealing with such issues. This is research on the ground knowing the area really well, working in the field, and conducting original scientific research. That is when we can use the tools we recently talked about, using the polls, questionnaires, and interviews, but only if they are standardised, unless they are being changed and unless they are arbitrary.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: When using the samples method, can the subjectivity of choosing specific municipalities can entail certain risks? [Microphone not activated] ... I apologise, my microphone was off and the interpreters have not heard me. Professor, if the selection of municipalities which are to be covered by the samples is subjective, does it entail the risk you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Yes, and your question is somewhat suggestive because whenever anyone is subjective then the picture you create about anything is different. If I selected a different sample of municipalities, you would see that the picture we would get would be completely different from what has been represented in this case. That means that subjectivity would have to be excluded in order to avoid creating false historical pictures concerning certain processes and phenomena. This is why I believe that a number of works dealing with this issue, and that is the purpose of my report, provide a more comprehensive and more realistic picture of what took place in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, at least with respect to the demographic aspect of the issue that we are discussing here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: When we discuss Bosnia-Herzegovina, do we have to take into account the entire territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina in order to arrive at valid data?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: From what I just answered when answering to your previous question, the answer is of course. The picture that is by far more realistic would be obtained if we covered the entire territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and represented by facts everything that was researched, all the phenomena and everything else. Then we would have the most relevant and the most comprehensive picture of everything that has to do with demographic processes, whatever is done partially, in terms of research in certain areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina, cannot provide such a picture. I claim this categorically and I can prove it factually at any given moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Does that have anything to do with the argument you mentioned, the argument concerning communicating vessels where the population shifts from one area to another and so on?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Of course. This is an additional argument considering that the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina within its borders and without the borders of Bosnia-Herzegovina is prone to movements. What illustrates this are two millions [as interpreted] of people who moved from their households at the beginning of the war, about 1 million left Bosnia-Herzegovina and another million within Bosnia-Herzegovina. This will be the category of the so-called displaced persons, around 1 million. That is sufficient to illustrate the principle which we call chain reaction or communicating vessels or something similar. This is why it is very difficult to prepare a sample and prove on a sample all the demographic issues in connection with this subject. MR. Di FAZIO: If Your Honours please, by now in the evidence we've heard that there's a principle of connected vessels which is also known as a principle call the domino effect, and now we find it's the -- furthermore, it has a third name, chain reaction. There's been, so far, and I'm not aware of anywhere in the report where this principle that goes by three names has been explained. In order for you to follow this evidence, you'll have to find out eventually at some point and I suggest now would be a good time, what exactly the principle of connected vessels or the domino effects or chain reaction exactly is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Professor, I will not repeat my learned friend the Prosecutor's question. Can you please explain what the Prosecutor is interested in.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: I have understood Mr. Prosecutor's question. I believe that in my previous answers, I tried to illustrate that by using an example. In addition to the three municipalities, i.e., Zavidovici, Kljuc and Sanski Most, I also included the example of the Bijeljina municipality, from where 24.000 Muslims moved out but at the same time 39.000 Serbs came to Bijeljina. From where, from Sarajevo, from Tuzla and from Zenica. I mean, these towns and the surrounding areas. Simultaneously, from Bijeljina, Zvornik, Banja Luka, Doboj and so on, the Muslim population moved out into the towns from which Serbs have moved to the listed towns. Likewise, the Croatian population oriented itself towards Mostar, Western Herzegovina and enclaves that I mentioned: Zepce, in Central Bosnia, and Odzak and Orasje in the Posavina region. However, the picture often changed during the war because some of the areas were, on several occasions, controlled by one or the other or the third military formation, let me put it that way. Symbolically, we called it, under quotation marks, communicating vessels or chain reactions, even though the expert terms that we used are not symbolic or figurative in that kind. The idea was to be as figurative as possible for a wider audience, and this is why we mention that here today. But I think that it was clear what is meant by the chain reaction or as Mr. Prosecutor called it, the domino effect. Something is torn down in one area, something is built up in another one. This is a demographic characteristic of movements of the population in Bosnia-Herzegovina, especially during war time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right, Professor. One ethnic group, if it moves out from a certain area and comes to another area where this ethnic group constitutes the majority, by moving in this way, does it exert pressure on other ethnic groups which then have to leave? Could that be the chain reaction process, as I understand it, and please correct me if I'm wrong?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that essentially you have understood the problem correctly. When due to the forced migration, a group of people from one ethnic group comes to one specific area, then indirectly pressure is exerted on another ethnic group who had been living there earlier. That ethnic group feels more insecure because war implies many terrible things, people have left their family members, some extremist or paramilitary groups appear and great insecurity is felt by the civilians, and then people were willing to leave everything they have, all their property and to go to territory which they would consider to be more safe which was most often an area where their ethnic group was predominant. This is what I called voluntary migration, and these are absolute characteristics of demographic movement in Bosnia-Herzegovina during the war between 1991 and 1995. And it peaked just before the outbreak of the war and during the initial period of the conflict, because later on the borders were closed, movements were made more difficult, and even if you wanted, you could not move from one area to another, it was impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Professor, have there been conditions after the war and up until now to make a study that would cover the entire territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that would deal with all the issues pertaining to demographic movements in Bosnia-Herzegovina during the war and up to this day?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Let me first say that there is a great need for such work. On the other hand, so far we have not managed to produce such a comprehensive study at the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina in order to determine all the facts. I primarily have in mind something that would be produced internally within Bosnia-Herzegovina by the local professionals and scientists who have not produced such a work. The most comprehensive research is believed to be the work of Ewa Tabeau and IDC, Mr. Tokaca, on the one hand; and in terms of the area of Republika Srpska, I think that would including my own remember search. This is why I emphasised in my report that if these three studies and many others that are necessary could somehow be integrated, we would get a quite different, more comprehensive, more realistic fact about all developments and demographic changes in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I can just announce along these lines that soon a book written by me will be published, so these three researches perhaps taken together might provide a more comprehensive research focused on Bosnia-Herzegovina that would be based on scientific facts without any impartiality or subjectivity which is not to be accepted in science, and without any compromise because there can be no compromise in science. That is acceptable in politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In such an effort, would you and everyone else striving to make such a report, the census would be of any help, the census which is being constantly talked about in Bosnia-Herzegovina and would be a good idea to produce such a study only once a census is conducted?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: As for the professionals from this field in Bosnia-Herzegovina, we have said a census is something that is most necessary at this moment. It should cover the territory of all of Bosnia-Herzegovina. After 20 years, it is really needed if we are to have valid statistical data. If I may just illustrate how important that is by giving another example. After the war, Croatia conducted a census in 2001 and faced all the other -- all the major demographic problems in that country. I think this is something that is necessary in Bosnia-Herzegovina as well. However, the issue of the population census in Bosnia-Herzegovina has shifted into the field of politics and it is now only a political issue. Once the law on the census is adopted and the political agreement has to be reached first, then the technical part of the census can be carried out quite easily and we expect this to take place next year at the latest. We would then enter another census decade as recommended by United Nations to all countries of the world so that the data would be included in international statistical databases that it could be compared and that various development programmes could be created. Without the census Bosnia-Herzegovina would have major problems in connection with this and also when it comes to accessing funds from the European Union, and so on, which would make its overall development quite difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. I will now move on to something else. Namely, Professor, in the introductory section of your report, you cite the examples of the Zavidovici, Kljuc and Sanski Most municipalities, and you note the decrease in the numbers of Muslims. First of all, I have to ask you whether Zavidovici was under the control of Muslim forces throughout the war? I have in mind only the Zavidovici municipality. And are they now part of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina? MR. Di FAZIO: If Your Honours please, unless I've misunderstood Mr. Cvijetic's question, the number of Bosniaks increased.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If that's how it's recorded then it's wrong. MR. Di FAZIO: Yeah, it says 34.198 in 1991 and 34.227 in 2009, according to this table. I want to make sure Dr. Pasalic has the correct figures when he is discussing this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree. I don't want to testify either and Professor Pasalic will explain that. But if you have carefully read the expert report, then you will see how this difference is accounted for.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Could you help us, Professor?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: I can explain to you based on the table, though it is explained in the text. Let's take Zavidovici municipality as our example. It had 57.164 inhabitants in 1991, of which number 34.198 Muslims. In 2009, the estimate is that the municipality had 38.027 inhabitants which means a decrease of about 19.000. Why? Because about 10.000 Serbs left and 5- to 6.000 Croats. We could say that this -- this is the compensation. We have said that about 10.000 displaced persons from Eastern Bosnia, mostly from Srebrenica, settled the area. I know that because I was born and grew up in that area. It was mostly populated by people from Srebrenica who were transferred there. If you see -- if you add these 10.000 then you see that 10.000 native Muslims were missing. Why? I have explained that as well. All three ethnic groups were leaving during the war but also after the war. Zavidovici municipality can even be taken as a representative example for the emigration of all three ethnic groups. The demographic losses of this municipality amount to almost 20.000, but this comprises all ethnic groups, including the one that was dominant before the war and remained dominant after the war. But the other ethnic groups also left during the war for economic reasons, for reasons of lack of security on safety. And I can mention another example, the Krivaja timber industry which was basically closed down and some 30.000 people were left without a job. That's why emigration was very strong here. That was the largest timber processing plant in former Yugoslavia. They had 12- to 14.000 employees overall, not only Zavidovici but also other places. They are out of business and certainly the native -- the local Muslims also left the area. I must also say the following : The absolute capacities of all ethnic groups in Bosnia-Herzegovina have diminished since the war. Relative indicators only change in local or regional areas so that the percentage of the Bosniaks in Zavidovici has now risen to about 90 per cent; however, the absolute human capacity is smaller than before the war. I'm now referring to the native population. This has created -- or rather, a distorted image has come to being by the arrival of displaced persons. In Bosnia-Herzegovina, this problem is only finally solved for about -- for a smaller number of persons. The international convention does not protect internally displaced persons. It's a matter that should be dealt with by their country as opposed to the issue of refugees who enjoy international protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Professor, let us try to corroborate your thesis about emigration with examples from Ms. Tabeau's book.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please see 65 ter 10368. 398, sorry. 10398. And that's now Exhibit P01627, if I'm not mistaken. Once we see it, I will give you your right page reference. Could we please go to page 81 in Serbian and page 72 in English. Page 72 in English and page 81 in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Professor, you don't have to look because the page numbers do not coincide with the page numbers in the electronic version. In your hard copy, it's page 85. But you can also see it on the screen, but I believe you'll see it better in the hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please enlarge the top. Actually, only the part of the text in bold type. No, I mean further down where the numbers are. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Professor, I would like to draw your attention to something in this table. It's titled -- it's part of Annex A1. We want to focus on the numbers here. The language isn't really an issue here because it's only the numbers we are interested in. Professor, look at the Muslims according to the 1991 census. The Muslims in the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the number is 375.522, can you see it?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let me point out to you that this is not the entire Federation, only nine municipalities that were dealt with in the Milosevic case, so don't get puzzled by the number. So this is the population in these nine municipalities, 375.522. MR. Di FAZIO: I object, if Your Honours please. The title needs to be read, "Status of 1991 and 1997, 1998: Individuals Born Before 1980." It's part of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, but I wanted to read it all. But I'm now focusing only on the numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let us now move on to 1997, 1998, Professor. And we can see a decrease of the absolute number of inhabitants to 268.745. Can you see that number?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: But in the last column where a percentage is stated, we can see an increase by 57.5 per cent in these nine municipalities. This is an increase in the share of the Muslims. At first sight this may be a mathematical paradox. Can you explain, could this be conclusion or could this follow from what you were saying a minute ago?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is exactly the case. The absolute demographic capacities were reduced, whereas the relative indicators have changed. If I may say, although it doesn't say so here, but I have research into this, the overall demographic losses in Bosnia-Herzegovina are about 800.000 from 1992 through 2010. That, of course, includes all ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Professor, but let's stick to the table for the time being -- MR. Di FAZIO: If Your Honours please. I am sorry to interrupt, but the way the transcript is coming out, it's misleading. If you look at those figures, they apply only to the Milosevic case area, they only apply to individuals born before 1980, and the figure of plus 57 per cent only applies to that part of the Milosevic municipalities that were studied that are in the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It's by no means related to nine municipalities or Bosnia-wide. It's very specific. If you just go horizontally across and you can see what that summary of figures means. Republika Srpska, percentage change in Muslims down by 95 per cent; in the Federation, up by 57. That is the area it's talking about and group within that Muslim population, namely those born before 1980. So you got to be precise now because these tables are trying to be as precise as they can, and you can't just simply have generalised questions and answers, otherwise you won't understand this table which is what this evidence is about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, and I speak entirely for myself, it seems to me that the -- and I confess my difficulty with figures such as this, but for comprehension, wouldn't it be simpler for Mr. Cvijetic to lead the evidence in the way that he understands it and you to reserve your matters for cross-examination? Wouldn't that make it more comprehensible for all of us? MR. Di FAZIO: Certainly, if you prefer me to approach it in that fashion, I'm happy to do that. But I'd just like to alert the Trial Chamber to the need for, when following the evidence, to look long and hard at these particular tables as the evidence proceeds. But I'll do it in the manner that you suggested --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You'll flag these tables when the come up and take us back to it at the appropriate time. MR. Di FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that the Prosecutor is anticipating my following questions. So I would just like to ask for a bit of patience and everything will be clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Professor, how and for what reason did the percentage of Muslims rise if the absolute number dropped so sharply? That would be my first question.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: If you listened to my previous answers carefully, this can all be subsumed under the process of ethnic territorial homogenisation, although I must immediately state some doubt with regard to these numbers which represent the share of the population that was born before 1980. To my mind, this is irrelevant, and I refuted that on using the examples of some municipalities because the calculations by which these numbers were arrived at were very simple or simplified. Why? Because the differences in natural population growth is such that the Muslims who have the greatest population growth obviously have the strongest group of -- the largest share in the younger population. That's why such a simplified image came into being. It is clear that the Muslim population settled in municipalities that belonged to the Federation, and although their absolute capacities were reduced, and I said that was because 800.000 people are missing from Bosnia-Herzegovina as compared to the previous census, then all relative indicators change and only they -- in the Federation, the Muslim populations are dominant here and the RS the Serbs, but both, and also the Croats, have a reduced absolute capacity. There are also official statistical data from the Federal Bureau of Statistics that are based on estimates, and these are identical. So this is just the shifting of population from one region to another for reasons of war losses, direct or indirect, purely demographic losses and also, of course, overall demographic losses. By way of conclusion, let me say that what was presented in Ewa Tabeau's report to my mind is irrelevant because more elements, criteria and factors should have been included to get more accurate data, especially for 1997, 1998, where the author herself stated that the results were arrived at based on some unreliable sources. That's very obvious and I agree with that absolutely, so that these numbers should not be taken for granted, although the overall trend is clear, namely the process of ethnic territorial homogenisation in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The essence of my question is the last thing you said, was this growth of the relative share of the Muslim population irrespective of the drop in their absolute number a result of the moving out of Serb and Croatian population in the area?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Certainly. We are talking about municipalities that are now part of the Federation of BH where the Serb population but also the Croatian population is the absolute minority. Although all groups' capacities have diminished, still the relative share of an ethnic group, in this case the Muslims, has grown in municipalities that belong to the Federation of BH. We can also speak about the reverse process, of course. I hope that this is sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: We will get to the opposite process as well, I'm interested in another piece of information now. Which of the factors affected the moving out of the Muslim population and the reduction in absolute numbers in the area that was under the Muslim control during the war and now remains within the territory of the Federation of BH?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I will repeat some of the data. During the war, there were numerous political, economic, social, psychological factors, and then after the war the dominant factors are the economic ones. These are the factors that cause the moving out of the population within the municipalities belonging to the Federation. I can corroborate this with the following data published by the Federal Bureau of Statistics. Not a single canton out of 10, except the Tuzla and Sarajevo canton, has the same number of residents as in 1991. All of them in absolute terms have fewer residents. Tuzla and Sarajevo have approximately the same number of residents. However, the relative indicators have changed and now the dominant population in all cantons but three are the Muslims, and in the three it's Croats that are dominant, Western Herzegovina canton, Posavina canton and Canton 10. It is visible that in these cantons, and if we add to it -- we can also add to it Podrinje canton, have a negative birth-rate or birth growth which means that Bosnia population has the largest share in all of these population structures because traditionally, both in former Yugoslavia and currently, that ethnic group has the largest growth rate or birth-rate even though it is now smaller than before the war. This is typical for many countries in Europe that have not completed demographic transition processes unlike some other European countries that have completed that process. So let me repeat once again, what is shown here in this report by Mrs. Tabeau cannot be relevant if we were to take into account all factors and facts that I spoke of when it comes to these matters. In this regard, we need to include a much broader selection of facts in order to come to the conclusions that would be of greater quality and validity.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. I will now give you an opportunity to give your final judgement on this, but before we get to that, please look at the column with the final numbers above the figure of 57.5 per cent. Right above it is minus 95.5 per cent which pertains to the number of Muslims in the Republika Srpska as compared to the 1991 census information. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do not comment on it now, just keep it in your mind for the time being while we move to page 89 in the Serbian version, since we are dealing with figures only now. Let's look at the column entitled "Serbs," please, and could we enlarge the bolded part, please. Excellent. Now, please, look at the situation with the Serbian population in the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Please go to the last column where we see the figure of minus 88.2 per cent. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Professor -- it's page 80 in English, for reference. With all doubts that you had concerning this data, if we were to compare these percentages, in the Federation, according to Ewa Tabeau, the number of Serbs has been reduced by 95.5 per cent, and in Republika Srpska, the number of Muslims was reduced by 88.2 per cent. So let me repeat the question that I already put to you: This piece of information, is it indicative with respect to your thesis on overflowing and shifts of population?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Let us be clear, please. When I spoke about the inaccuracy of this data, it pertained to these figures which I assert are not fully accurate. However, I did not mean to challenge the process which took place in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the process of movement of population towards dominantly populated regions for each ethnic group, and this process confirms this. If we were to analyse percentages nowadays, we would get a completely different picture. For example, let me confirm this for you. According to the Federal Bureau of Statistics in the Federation, there are currently 4 per cent of Serbs living. In 1991, and you have that information before you, there were 17.6 per cent of Serbs or near 500.000 Serbs living in the same territory of the Federation. As for Muslims in Republika Srpska, according to 1991 census, there were about 28 per cent of them; whereas in the sample offered by Ms. Tabeau, we see the figure of 30, 32 per cent of Muslims that had left the area of Republika Srpska. This is why this is not accurate data. This is the principle of territorial ethnic homogenisation of ethnic groups which shows us that there was a transfer of population. Sometimes it was caused by ethnic cleansing, sometimes it was caused by deportations and prosecution. I've already explained that to you. These processes continue to this day. In Republika Srpska, we have a different picture nowadays, I'll show you figures later on, and you will see that some 200.000 residents of other ethnic groups returned to Republika Srpska which is about 20 per cent of its total population. And if we remember that the Federation is composed of Muslims and Croats and that they currently comprise 95 per cent of total population, and there are about 4 per cent of Serbs and 1 per cent of others, then we see that this process of return and change of ethnic picture in Federation lags behind the same processes in Republika Srpska. So the picture is changing in both entities, but right now it is more positive in the territory of Republika Srpska. I am speaking on the basis of information that come from the Federal Bureau for Statistics so that there's no doubt about this information being biased or you should not have any doubts because this information does not come from Republika Srpska, it comes from the Federation. And I'm here to answer any of the questions you may have.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Since we are going move to another topic tomorrow, let us now conclude with this topic, Professor. Therefore, in the territory of the Federation, we see a drop in the absolute figures of Muslim population. This is beyond dispute. And you say that there is such a trend in the entire Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is to say that this trend is observed in Republika Srpska as well, did I get it right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Yes, you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Now, during war, was the war itself as a force majeure something that contributed to these trends and to what extent?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC
utterances.text: Naturally. Not only in Bosnia and Herzegovina but elsewhere as well. The war is the strongest motive for transfer of population. Given that 2 million residents of Bosnia-Herzegovina moved about, one million going outside of Bosnia-Herzegovina and one million shifting within Bosnia-Herzegovina, that shows that due to political, economic -- or rather, in addition to political, economic and social factors, the war was the greatest factor effecting movement of population. But what is even more important is that even after the war, the demographic figures in Bosnia-Herzegovina continued to drop in the entire territory and also in certain regions because there is not a single municipality in the entire Bosnia-Herzegovina that has the same number of residents as before the war except for very few exceptions, such as densely populated urban areas, Sarajevo, Banja Luka and Bijeljina in the Republika Srpska. All other regions in Bosnia-Herzegovina registered a drop in human resources, and that in itself caused relative changes, caused what we described as ethnic territorial homogenisation in certain areas, that is to say that there was a redistribution of population within Bosnia-Herzegovina itself. These are the evident trends that have been present in Bosnia-Herzegovina since 1992 until nowadays.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I want to move to some other topics, namely to the expert report of Professor Pasalic, so please don't be upset that I ask that we finish for the day. It will not affect the final estimate of time that I told you I needed for his examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cvijetic. Professor Pasalic, we are about to take the adjournment for today, the first day of your testimony. And at this stage, I would point out to you that having been sworn as a witness, you cannot have any communication with counsel from either side in the matter until you are released by the Court. Moreover, in such conversations as you may have with persons outside of the Chamber, you cannot discuss your testimony. Do you understand what I've just said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I have understood it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. So we take the adjournment. Reconvene tomorrow morning at 9.00.
